title: Why settled Vikings deserve our attention
gist: Katherine Harvey reviews Neil Price's The Sea-King and the Sorceress, which profiles 21 individuals from across the Viking diaspora to argue that 'Viking' was a job description rather than an identity and that most Norse people were settled farmers. Archaeological evidence such as sex-skewed cemeteries, malnutrition patterns, care for the disabled, slavery and sorcery burials shows a society that does not fit modern stereotypes.

insights.claim: Archaeologist Neil Price argues that the Old Norse word 'víkingr', meaning something like 'pirate', was a job description rather than an ethnic identity, and that it misdescribes a population made up mostly of settled farmers.
insights.so_what: Popular historical brands often rest on modern fantasy rather than evidence, which is relevant to heritage and media IP built on Viking imagery.
insights.quote: the Old Norse word ‘víkingr’ (which means something like ‘pirate’) is more of a job description than an ethnic identity
insights.locator: As a Christian woman who lived
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey

insights.claim: Price contends that modern expectations of Vikings are shaped chiefly by our own fantasies and preoccupations rather than by the evidence of how most of them lived.
insights.so_what: A reminder that popular narratives can diverge sharply from the underlying data.
insights.locator: As a Christian woman who lived
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey

insights.claim: In the Danish farming community of Randlev, 80% of excavated graves belong to women, which suggests many local men went raiding or trading and died elsewhere.
insights.so_what: Shows how mass male labour migration or military service reshapes the demography of home communities.
insights.quote: 80 per cent of the excavated graves belong to women
insights.locator: Further evidence of the domestic impact
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey

insights.claim: Childhood malnutrition was far more common among females throughout the Viking world, almost certainly because sons were prioritised when food was scarce.
insights.so_what: Historical evidence of gender bias in allocating scarce resources under stress.
insights.quote: if there was not enough food, sons were prioritised
insights.locator: Further evidence of the domestic impact
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey

insights.claim: Viking trading centres such as Birka, where more than 1,000 graves have been excavated, operated at the same time as the raids, and some plundered jewellery there may have rewarded people who financed raiders.
insights.so_what: Suggests early private financing of raiding ventures, a proto-investment model.
insights.quote: perhaps, he suggests, she had provided financial support to the raiders, and the jewellery was her reward?
insights.locator: Many others lived more settled lives
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey

insights.claim: Viking society practised infant exposure according to sagas and law codes, yet a brother and sister with a rare form of dwarfism buried in late-11th-century Skömsta were clearly well cared for and integrated into their community.
insights.so_what: Societies hold contradictory attitudes toward the vulnerable, which complicates simple historical generalisations.
insights.locator: Such sexism is what we expect
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey

insights.claim: Slavery was common in the Viking world and thralls were often killed during funeral rituals, as in an Isle of Man grave where a young woman was killed by a single blow while kneeling.
insights.so_what: Underlines the role of slavery in Viking economies and status display.
insights.quote: it is true that slavery was common in the Viking world, and thralls were quite often killed during funeral rituals
insights.locator: The identity of the Oseberg women
insights.speaker: Katherine Harvey
